an9.34:1.1: I have heard that on one occasion Ven. Sāriputta was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Forest, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.
an9.34:1.2: There he said to the monks,
an9.34:1.5: When this was said, Ven. Udāyin said to Ven. Sāriputta,
an9.34:1.6: “But what is the pleasure here, my friend, where there is nothing felt?”
an9.34:1.7: “Just that is the pleasure here, my friend: where there is nothing felt.
an9.34:1.8: There are these five strands of sensuality.
an9.34:1.10: Forms cognizable via the eye—agreeable, pleasing, charming, endearing, enticing, linked to sensual desire;
an9.34:1.14: tactile sensations cognizable via the body—agreeable, pleasing, charming, endearing, enticing, linked to sensual desire.
an9.34:1.16: Whatever pleasure or joy arises in dependence on these five strands of sensuality, that is sensual pleasure.
an9.34:2.1: “Now there is the case where a monk—quite secluded from sensuality, secluded from unskillful qualities—enters & remains in the first jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by directed thought & evaluation.
an9.34:2.2: If, as he remains there, he is beset with attention to perceptions dealing with sensuality, that is an affliction for him.
an9.34:2.3: Just as pain would arise in a healthy person as an affliction,
an9.34:2.4: even so the attention to perceptions dealing with sensuality that beset the monk is an affliction for him.
an9.34:2.5: Now, the Blessed One has said that whatever is an affliction is stress.
an9.34:2.6: So by this line of reasoning it may be known how unbinding is pleasant.
an9.34:3.1: “Then there is the case where a monk, with the stilling of directed thoughts & evaluations, enters & remains in the second jhāna: rapture & pleasure born of concentration, unification of awareness free from directed thought & evaluation—internal assurance.
an9.34:3.2: If, as he remains there, he is beset with attention to perceptions dealing with directed thought, that is an affliction for him.…
an9.34:4.1: “Then there is the case where a monk, with the fading of rapture, remains equanimous, mindful, & alert, senses pleasure with the body, and enters & remains in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous & mindful, he has a pleasant abiding.’
an9.34:4.2: If, as he remains there, he is beset with attention to perceptions dealing with rapture, that is an affliction for him.…
an9.34:5.1: “Then there is the case where a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure & pain—as with the earlier disappearance of elation & distress—enters & remains in the fourth jhāna: purity of equanimity & mindfulness, neither pleasure nor pain.
an9.34:5.2: If, as he remains there, he is beset with attention to perceptions dealing with equanimity, that is an affliction for him.…
an9.34:6.1: “Then there is the case where a monk, with the complete transcending of perceptions of (physical) form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of multiplicity, (perceiving,) ‘Infinite space,’ enters & remains in the dimension of the infinitude of space.
an9.34:6.2: If, as he remains there, he is beset with attention to perceptions dealing with form, that is an affliction for him.…
an9.34:7.1: “Then there is the case where a monk, with the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of space, (perceiving,) ‘Infinite consciousness,’ enters & remains in the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness.
an9.34:7.2: If, as he remains there, he is beset with attention to perceptions dealing with the dimension of the infinitude of space, that is an affliction for him.…
an9.34:8.1: “Then there is the case where a monk, with the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness, (perceiving,) ‘There is nothing,’ enters & remains in the dimension of nothingness.
an9.34:8.2: If, as he remains there, he is beset with attention to perceptions dealing with the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness, that is an affliction for him.…
an9.34:9.1: “Then there is the case where a monk, with the complete transcending of the dimension of nothingness, enters & remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.
an9.34:9.2: If, as he remains there, he is beset with attention to perceptions dealing with the dimension of nothingness, that is an affliction for him.
an9.34:9.5: Now, the Blessed One has said that whatever is an affliction is stress.
an9.34:9.6: So by this line of reasoning it may be known how unbinding is pleasant.
an9.34:10.1: “Then there is the case where a monk, with the complete transcending of the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters & remains in the cessation of perception & feeling. And as he sees (that) with discernment, effluents are completely ended.
an9.34:11.1: So by this line of reasoning it may be known how unbinding is pleasant.”
